questions.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation ${x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=6?$
questions.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form. 

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $2{y}_{1}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the given curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1}^{2} & =6 \\ {y}_{1}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

This represents the two parallel lines ${y}_{1}=\sqrt{3}$ and ${y}_{1}=-\sqrt{3}.$

Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}+10{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.  

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 5 \\ 5 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda -16 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =8,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $8{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2}.$  

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$

$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes  $2$ and $4.$

questions.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=11.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=11
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-5)I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]+5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-5)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

canonical_examples.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2= 70?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2.$ To  determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(\mathbf{x})$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ which is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/2d7e7ed4884b98bd6258ed6e3752f9b6bf1e779041e769ca0e177f8b9b385a50.svg)

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & -9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -70 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =7,\,-10\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $7y_1^2 -10 y_2^2.$  

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{y}_{1}^{2}-10{y}_{2}^{2} & =70 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{10}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{7} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{10})^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{7})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $\sqrt{10}$ and $\sqrt{7}.$

A \mathbf{x} = 1.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=1,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 1
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/9d5eb1eefa424b5ff9c333542b4f716e7143c373acc117717468e1c8001a734f.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get

- For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Example: 
                    Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve
canonical_examples.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $19x_1^2-6x_1x_2+11x_2^2 = 20.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=19x_1^2-6x_1x_2+11x_2^2.$ The matrix of the form is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/f408697d4afc249d6dcb4254618cf03e064c400d87e31c8a6c6055ccf9d70d7e.svg)

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 20
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I| = 0,$ we obtain

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=20 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=10.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For $\lambda_2=20,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-20I & =[\begin{aligned}19 & -3 \\ -3 & 11\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-20I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/0442c5fae9cb761b85a9c5be308b79dfc1ff05b379912f0e8d42cb724da947b4.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/3ff0045c806703fac9f102b44c7e2031c0b5095ac48e122f87947a471f650641.svg)

- For $\lambda_1=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}19 & -3 \\ -3 & 11\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/7c8822cb00d532e85b62b4b299b2a2ab47f13928d4ff21bca78413f9df631152.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/ad6348443131aa88232fb0a1d82f7c7ef5fdea6ac5f27addcbe52d891e45b995.svg)

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/5118522a8ac8351d9657f6bf6ed82b838347944141c11fd43977e53ac48b7e24.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/40b663f947e3705fa2a9d2b1fa99634cf76bed6622c11d54bbc7029a40c193d1.svg)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix with real entries. As we know, there exists an orthonormal change of variables 

$$
\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}
$$

that transforms the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ into the quadratic form $\mathbf{y}^TD\mathbf{y},$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. 

The columns of the matrix $P$ are the (normalized) unit eigenvectors of $A,$ which are mutually orthogonal. These are called the **principal axes** of the quadratic form.

Let's use this knowledge to find out which curve is defined by the equation 

$$
6x_1^2+4x_1x_2+3x_2^2= 14,
$$

and see the geometric interpretation of the principal axes.

If we plot our curve using a graphical calculator, we obtain the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/d8a6b6dff52e0c4004432f9447b5fd484612eaacf07588c3469af143b0a9e880.png)

It looks like an ellipse. Let's now find our coordinate system, in which the equation of the curve will be the simplest.

First, we consider the corresponding quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})={\color{blue}6}x_1^2+{\color{red}4}x_1x_2+{\color{blue}3}x_2^2,
$$

which we reduce to its canonical (diagonal) form. 

So, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}) \mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/2a4229ed50ef304e06cec6a64a3fa522a0aa679b70ebc1608b9042aedbbed2ef.svg)

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +14 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =7,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the principal axes of the curve.

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/85e44a8dc5afeda8a266dca013f4298e7e475ea6ce7808cfe3072b4b23186334.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/81c9b8b9f946e7c427bae2c1a7efa0a57c9f0388c9d67d846a14971bf9f33902.svg)

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/d62eeed8be7829fc1d145697fb700d5f282ceaf45c3d967a8cb1270b4399f906.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/6123f9b7e7cce970066dea2ab36a4e1d2704a17af961d03e016d83683eb13124.svg)

Therefore, the principal axes of our quadratic form (and the corresponding curve) are

$\qquad$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/f10b4edf9545e958d4f32a695da26077c1ab7baf096c0956f1e02ba9ec94c8bd.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/04a614acc9a6be123cdd1a8c765853a822da12f07137baaefef9f4715c59a5f3.svg)

Notice that in the diagram below, the principal axes correspond to the axes $y_1$ and $y_2.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/10a2f0ccd179eba7f65410f932548d954a459e1bc8dcb0803a5b2d9fe7896432.png)

In the new coordinate system, our quadratic form can be reduced to 

$$
7y_1^2 + 2y_2^2.
$$

 

Therefore, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2} & =14 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{7})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt{7}.$

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix with real entries. As we know, there exists an orthonormal change of variables 

$$
\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}
$$

that transforms the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ into the quadratic form $\mathbf{y}^TD\mathbf{y},$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. 

The columns of the matrix $P$ are the (normalized) unit eigenvectors of $A,$ which are mutually orthogonal. These are called the **principal axes** of the quadratic form.

Let's use this knowledge to find out which curve is defined by the equation 

$$
6x_1^2+4x_1x_2+3x_2^2= 14,
$$

and see the geometric interpretation of the principal axes.

If we plot our curve using a graphical calculator, we obtain the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/d8a6b6dff52e0c4004432f9447b5fd484612eaacf07588c3469af143b0a9e880.png)

It looks like an ellipse. Let's now find our coordinate system, in which the equation of the curve will be the simplest.

First, we consider the corresponding quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})={\color{blue}6}x_1^2+{\color{red}4}x_1x_2+{\color{blue}3}x_2^2,
$$

which we reduce to its canonical (diagonal) form. 

So, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}) \mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/2a4229ed50ef304e06cec6a64a3fa522a0aa679b70ebc1608b9042aedbbed2ef.svg)

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +14 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =7,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the principal axes of the curve.

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/85e44a8dc5afeda8a266dca013f4298e7e475ea6ce7808cfe3072b4b23186334.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/81c9b8b9f946e7c427bae2c1a7efa0a57c9f0388c9d67d846a14971bf9f33902.svg)

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/d62eeed8be7829fc1d145697fb700d5f282ceaf45c3d967a8cb1270b4399f906.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/6123f9b7e7cce970066dea2ab36a4e1d2704a17af961d03e016d83683eb13124.svg)

Therefore, the principal axes of our quadratic form (and the corresponding curve) are

$\qquad$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/f10b4edf9545e958d4f32a695da26077c1ab7baf096c0956f1e02ba9ec94c8bd.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/04a614acc9a6be123cdd1a8c765853a822da12f07137baaefef9f4715c59a5f3.svg)

Notice that in the diagram below, the principal axes correspond to the axes $y_1$ and $y_2.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228956/assets/10a2f0ccd179eba7f65410f932548d954a459e1bc8dcb0803a5b2d9fe7896432.png)

In the new coordinate system, our quadratic form can be reduced to 

$$
7y_1^2 + 2y_2^2.
$$

 

Therefore, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2} & =14 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{7})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt{7}.$

tutorials.name: Some Special Cases
tutorials.problem:
In some special cases, a quadratic equation might generate a degenerate curve or even an empty set.

- For example, consider the quadratic equation 

$$
-3x_1^2+8x_1x_2+3x_2^2 = 0.
$$

Reducing the left-hand side to the canonical form, we obtain

$$
5y_1^2 - 5y_2^2 = 0
$$

which represents two intersecting lines $y_1 = y_2$ and $y_1 = -y_2.$

- Now consider the quadratic equation 

$$
-2x_1^2+8x_1x_2-8x_2^2 = 10.
$$

Reducing the left-hand side to the canonical form, we obtain

$$
- 10y_2^2 =10
$$

which represents an empty set as the equation $y_2^2 = -1$ does not have any real solution.

- Finally, reducing the left-hand side of 

$$
x_1^2-4x_1x_2+4x_2^2 = 5
$$

to the canonical form, we obtain

$$
5y_2^2 =5
$$

which represents a pair of parallel lines $y_2 = 1$ and $y_2=-1.$
